## In Class

- 📽️ [**Deck 02 — What is a Computer?**](../materials/w01-deck-02-what-is-a-computer.html) — Tuesday's slides. They separate four things that are often confused: computing, which is a process; a computer, which is a machine; programming, which is what you do; and computational thinking, which is a way of approaching problems. The deck then covers the stored-program idea, which is what distinguishes a computer from earlier calculating machines.
- 🖨️ [**Hello, World — all the way down**](../materials/w01-hello-under-the-hood.html) — the closing demonstration, in two parts. First, `printf("abba")` in a world with only two letters, where a is 0 and b is 1, so the text stored in memory is just 0 1 1 0. Then the same five-instruction program, with the character set extended to ASCII, printing `Hello, world!`. The question it answers is why the number 72 means the letter H.
- 🐢 [**The Turtle Computer**](../materials/w01-turtle-computer.html) — your first programming language. It has ten words and one turtle, and requires no typing. We start here rather than with C, because it makes three points clearly: a program is a precise plan; the machine does exactly what you wrote, not what you intended; and features of a language get invented because some problem needed them.

## PAGAL Notes

*PAGAL — Perspectives on Algorithms, Generative AI & Learning: the week's informal column.*

- 📽️ **In slides:** [PAGAL — Programming in the Age of AI](../materials/w01-pagal-age-of-ai.html) — this week's column as a presentation. It covers what has changed in how software is written, the Specify–Verify loop, why the work is shifting from writing code to designing and checking systems, and what computing looks like inside other disciplines. The written version follows below.

**On telescopes, and on checking your quotes.**

This week's deck uses a well-known line: *"Computer science is not about machines, in the same way that astronomy is not about telescopes."*

Search for it and you will be told confidently that Edsger Dijkstra said it. So will framed posters, and so will several AI assistants. We checked, and that attribution does not hold up. The trail is documented at [Quote Investigator](https://quoteinvestigator.com/2021/04/02/computer-science/). Alan Perlis was making the telescope comparison as early as 1968. The closest early match in print is by the science writer George Johnson in 1986. The polished modern wording belongs to the mathematician **Michael Fellows**, writing with Ian Parberry in the early 1990s. Dijkstra would probably have agreed with it, but there is no verified record of him saying it.

Why begin a programming course with this? Because it is the same problem you will face all semester in a different form. A claim can be plausible, widely repeated, and still wrong, and the only way to find out is to check it against a source.

You will do exactly this with programs. The question is not "does this code look right?" but "does it do what was asked?" It is not "the AI said so" but "show me the evidence." The habit is the same in both cases.

As for the line itself, it survives the correction. You demonstrated it this week without noticing: you programmed a turtle, with no computer involved at all, and everything that mattered was the plan.

---

**Programming in the age of AI: what is our job now?**

For about seventy years the arrangement was that humans thought and computers executed. That arrangement has changed. A computer can now write a program, run it, and make a reasonable attempt at checking it. So it is worth asking directly what you are here to learn for four months.

Start with the economics. Programmers were paid well because writing software was scarce: few people could do it, and the world wanted more of it than they could produce. That scarcity is disappearing. Someone with no training can describe an application and get working code. When a machine can do something quickly and often well, that thing becomes a commodity, and careers are not built on commodities.

But look at which part the machine took over. Think of the work as three steps:

| Step | What it means | Who does it now |
|---|---|---|
| **Specify** | decide what should exist, and state it precisely enough that nothing is ambiguous | you |
| **Express** | turn that statement into code | increasingly the machine |
| **Verify** | judge whether what came back is correct, including at the edges and when it fails | you |

The machine took the middle step. It did not take the other two.

Be careful with the claim that the machine can verify its own work. A check is only ever a check against a specification. If you never stated the specification precisely, then the machine is checking against its own guess at what you wanted. The verification is worth exactly as much as the specification behind it.

This changes what you need to become good at. Two things in particular.

The first is thinking in systems: how parts connect, where they can fail, and what each part promises the others.

The second is reading. You will need to understand code you did not write, quickly and sceptically, because most of the code you deal with will arrive written by something else. You cannot check what you cannot read, and you cannot read it properly without understanding what is underneath it. That is why this course does not skip pointers, memory or the compiler.

The rule that follows from all of this is: **do not outsource the thinking.** Outsource the typing as much as you like. But if the problem statement, the plan and the judgement of correctness all come from the machine as well, then you are not using a tool. Everything in this course — the spec cards, the *given* and *ensures* habit, predicting output before running it, asking for evidence — is practice at the two steps that remain yours.

There is also a change that is not a skill. When answers are cheap, the scarce thing is the person who still asks questions. It has never been easier to look competent without understanding anything: accept the generated code, ship it, move on. Which is why the person who asks "but why does this work?", and who attempts a problem the hard way once before accepting the easy way, ends up further ahead. The machine will do your thinking. It will not do your wondering.

---

**A note on where problems come from.**

We drew the chain in class as *problem → plan → notation → executor*. But problems do not appear from nowhere. They belong to someone: a farmer pricing crops, a lab measuring an alloy, a clerk closing accounts. So the chain really begins one step earlier:

> world → problem → plan → notation → executor

A program is a claim about some part of the world: this is what mattered, and this is what should happen. If you get the world wrong, everything after it is efficiently and correctly wrong.

That gives two different questions, and they are worth keeping separate:

| Question | What it asks | Who can answer it |
|---|---|---|
| Did we build the thing **right**? | does the program meet the specification | tests can, and increasingly so can machines |
| Did we build the **right thing**? | does the specification serve the world it came from | only someone who knows that world |

The machine is becoming very good at the first question. The second one it cannot attempt, because it has never met the person whose problem this is.

This is why we keep insisting that you know your own discipline properly, and why writing a specification is not paperwork. A specification is a compressed description of someone else's situation, and writing a good one requires asking, listening, and caring whose problem it is. The turtle made this point too: the satisfaction never came from the program running. It came from the drawing matching what you intended.
